# Animal-powered machines (horse gin, treadwheel) (`animal_power_gin`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Deps: helped by gears_gear_trains, horse_collar_harness
- Core idea: An animal walking in a circle pulls a beam that turns a vertical shaft; a gear or a rope drum takes the power off to a mill, pump or mine hoist. A horse sustains roughly 500 to 700 watts over a working shift, a man on a treadwheel or crank about 75 to 100 watts, so one horse does the work of six to eight men. This is the yardstick every engine is measured against: Watt's "horsepower" (33,000 foot-pounds per minute, 746 W) was set deliberately above what an average horse delivers, and the first Newcomen engine of about 5 horsepower replaced a team of some twenty horses worked in shifts.
- Pitfalls:
  - Assuming a horse delivers one horsepower all day; sustained output is nearer two thirds of that
  - Too small a walking circle: under about 8 m diameter the animal pulls badly and goes lame
  - Forgetting the fodder: a working horse eats the produce of about two hectares
- History: greece: c. 3rd–2nd c. BC – animal-driven rotary mills spread in the Mediterranean; geared water-lifting wheel (saqiya) in Hellenistic Egypt; rome: 1st c. AD – donkey mills at Pompeii; treadwheel cranes; china: Han dynasty (206 BC–220 AD) – animal-driven mills; ox-driven hoists at the Sichuan brine wells; islamic: 8th–13th c. – saqiya standard for irrigation from Spain to India; al-Jazari describes animal-driven pumps (1206); europe: 15th–16th c. – horse whims drain and wind mines (Agricola 1556); in use at collieries into the 19th c.
- Read:
  - Georgius Agricola, De re metallica (1556; tr. H. C. Hoover & L. H. Hoover, 1912), Book VI
  - Vaclav Smil, Energy and Civilization: A History (2017)
